key_terms.أَهْلُ الْحَلِّ وَالْعَقْدِ: those having a say (people of authority)

ai.seo_question: How do Shia scholars view the enforcement of divine penalties during the occultation of the Imam?
ai.summary: This passage contrasts the juristic views of Abu Ali and Abu Hashim regarding the continuity of divine law during the Major Occultation, specifically addressing whether the removal of the 'excuse of ignorance' (uzr) depends on the Imam's physical presence. Abu Ali maintains that Allah directly sustains the authority to enforce limits and remove the excuse of the obligated, ensuring the continuity of religious obligation, whereas Abu Hashim views the application of penalties as a worldly administrative matter distinct from core theological doctrine. This debate highlights the Shia scholarly effort to reconcile the absence of the Imam with the ongoing validity of Shariah enforcement.

en.sayyid-athar-husain-s-h-rizvi: Abu Ali  has argued that in the conditions in which “those having a say” are not able to select an Imam, Allah performs acts that stand in place of enforcing the penalties and take away the excuse of duty-bound; and Abu Hashim  has said that enforcing penalties is a worldly matter and has no relationship with religion.
